u1l1: Look for a small bug at home or outside and count its legs together from a distance: is it an insect?
u1l2: Draw an insect together on a sheet of paper and mark the head, thorax and abdomen in three colors.
u1l3: Look out of the window or at a plant: do you see an insect flying? Guess how many wings it has.
u1l4: With your eyes closed, have an adult let you smell something from the kitchen. Guess it like an insect with its antennae!
u1l5: At mealtime, think about which insect mouth you'd use for each food: chewing, sucking or piercing?
u2l1: Take a walk around the house or neighborhood and write down three places where an insect could live.
u2l2: Invent a secret family signal with lights or claps, like fireflies, to call each other.
u2l3: Tell someone in your family the four stages of a butterfly, with a gesture for each one.
u2l4: Ask an adult if they've ever seen a small grasshopper without wings: it was a nymph!
u3l1: Look for a butterfly or a moth together and check its antennae: knob or feather?
u3l2: Find something at home that works like elytra, for example a box with a lid or a case. Open and close it: the hard lid is like the elytra, which protect, and what is inside is like the thin wings the beetle unfolds to fly. Then draw a beetle with its elytra open.
u3l3: At breakfast, count how many foods on the table exist thanks to bees.
u3l4: If you go to a river or a pond, look together for dragonflies near the water.
u3l5: Measure how far you jump and work out how far you'd jump if you were a grasshopper (about twenty times your size).
u3l6: If you hear a cicada singing, tell someone it's the male making its body vibrate.
u3l7: Check together that the food at home is covered, so flies don't land on it.
u4l1: Make a family list of what you wouldn't eat if there were no pollinating insects.
u4l2: Look for aphids on a plant and see if there are ladybugs nearby: biological control in action!
u4l3: Check the house together and empty still water from buckets, vases or tires so mosquitoes can't hatch.
u4l4: Explain to your family why almost all insects are friends, and how to stay safe from the few that sting.
u5l1: Ask your grandparents or aunts and uncles which part of Venezuela they come from and what insects they saw there as children.
u5l2: Ask at home if anyone has seen cocuyos and what they were called in their hometown. Did they know people once used them for light?
u5l3: For a week, watch the butterflies that pass by the garden, the park or the window. Write down their colors without catching them. Does any of them have an 88?
u5l4: Ask your family if anyone knows angelita honey or has seen the wax entrance of its nest on a wall or a tree.
u5l5: Play praying mantis: stay still as statues for one minute, with your arms folded. Hunting by waiting is hard!
u5l6: Plant a flowering plant together in a pot or in the yard, and watch for a week which insects visit it.
u6l1: Look for a small critter at home or outside and count its legs together from a distance: 6, 8, 14 or lots and lots? Is it an insect or a cousin?
u6l2: Look for a spider web together in a corner of the house or yard. Is any insect caught in it? Look at it without breaking it or touching the spider.
u6l3: Tell your family how to take a spider out of the house with a glass and a piece of card, and agree on which adult will do it if one shows up.
u6l4: With an adult, look for millipedes among the dry leaves in the garden or under a flowerpot. How many did you find? Leave them where they were.
u6l5: For a week, shake out your shoes as a family before putting them on: it's a good habit in case a scorpion or a spider found a dark corner to sleep in!
u6l6: Play a guessing game: one person describes a critter by its legs and body parts, and the others guess whether it's an insect or a cousin.
u7l1: Look together out of the window or outside for an animal that eats insects: a bird, a lizard or, at dusk, a bat.
u7l2: Open a fruit together (a mango, a passion fruit or a tomato) and find its seeds: that fruit came from a pollinated flower!
u7l3: Make a little recycling corner: a pile of dry leaves and peels in a corner of the yard or in a flowerpot, and look together every week at how it changes.
u7l4: Play color hide-and-seek: hide a green object and a red one among the plants. Which one is found first?
u7l5: Share out a day's jobs like a colony: who brings the food, who cooks and who cleans? It works better as a team!
u7l6: Plant a flowering plant together in a pot or in the yard for the pollinators, even a tiny one.
u8l1: Sit together for 5 minutes by a plant or a window and write down everything you see and hear. Who discovered the most things?
u8l2: At mealtime, have everyone ask a question about the insects at home and say what they think will happen. Pick one to check!
u8l3: With an adult, look under a dry leaf in the sun and under another in the shade. Where are there more little bugs? Put them back the way they were.
u8l4: Look around the house for insect hotel materials: canes, pine cones, twigs. Where would you put it?
u8l5: Choose one action together for this week: plant a flower in a pot or turn off the outdoor lights you aren't using.
u8l6: Make the forest ranger promise together: everyone says what they'll do to take care of insects. Write it down and stick it on the fridge!
